report:
**Conclusion:** For most people, regularly taking vitamin C does **not meaningfully prevent getting colds**. The best evidence—a Cochrane review of 29 comparisons involving 11,306 participants—found no effect on cold incidence in the ordinary population. It may, however, modestly shorten and lessen colds once they occur (about 8% shorter in adults and 14% in children).

There is a possible exception for people under short periods of intense physical stress or extreme cold (for example, endurance athletes or military personnel), in whom trials found fewer colds. This does not establish a general benefit for the public.

So, eating a vitamin-C-containing diet is sensible, but routine high-dose vitamin C specifically to prevent colds is generally not justified. High supplemental doses can cause gastrointestinal symptoms and may be unsuitable for some people (e.g., those prone to kidney stones); discuss supplements with a clinician if relevant.

Sources:  
- https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD000980_vitamin-c-preventing-and-treating-common-cold  
- https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23440782/  
- https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/providers/digest/the-common-cold-and-complementary-health-approaches  
- https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/VitaminC-HealthProfessional/
